headline: GLMZ EZA Files Class II Economic Zone Redesignation Application with United Nations Commerce Authority
source: GLMZ Economic Zone Authority — Public Communications Division
body:
The Great Lakes Metropolitan Zone Economic Zone Authority has submitted application EZA-2224-UNREQ-7 to the United Nations Commerce Authority requesting formal redesignation of [[GLMZ]] from Class I (Domestic Economic Zone) to Class II ([[CRUCIBLE Auric Sovereign Bespoke Arm|Sovereign]] Economic Zone). The application was received by UNCA on March 17, 2224, and confirmed as administratively complete on March 24, 2224.

The Class II designation would extend [[GLMZ]]'s existing regulatory authority to include expanded jurisdictional protocols governing cross-border commercial operations, inter-corponation dispute arbitration mechanisms, and infrastructure investment classification under UNCA standards. The designation would not alter existing internal sovereign territory arrangements within [[GLMZ]] or modify the authority of individual corponation sovereign territories over their designated zones.

'[[GLMZ]] currently accounts for 18.2 percent of [[Compass Rose|North]] American GDP as measured under Federal Remnant accounting standards,' said [[GLMZ]] EZA Director Maren Dahl-[[Franco Raghavan|Fontaine]] in the Authority's prepared statement. 'The Class I designation reflects [[GLMZ]]'s status in 2189. The Class II application reflects [[GLMZ]]'s status in 2224. The UNCA redesignation process was designed for exactly this evolution in zone scale and governance complexity.'

The application carries endorsements from fourteen of [[GLMZ]]'s Big 20 corponation bloc members. [[Sable Keïta-Suzuki|Ironclad]], Ringo, and Zheng-Dao declined to submit endorsement documentation. The three corporations have published a joint technical objection citing concerns about UNCA oversight provisions that would apply to cross-zone commercial dispute resolution — specifically the Class II requirement that corponations holding sovereign territory within a redesignated zone submit to UNCA arbitration as a condition of participation in zone-level trade compacts. Legal analysts note this objection is consistent with [[Sable Keïta-Suzuki|Ironclad]]'s longstanding position opposing any external arbitration mechanism applied to its sovereign territory operations.

The remaining three Big 20 members submitted conditional endorsements pending clarification of application language regarding the classification status of ungoverned and contested zones within [[GLMZ]]. The EZA's supplemental filing addressing ungoverned zone classification is expected in Q2 2224.

UNCA standard review timeline for Class II applications is 18 to 36 months. The [[GLMZ]] EZA anticipates a preliminary determination no earlier than Q3 2225.

Residents should note that the redesignation application does not affect current tier classifications, residency documentation, healthcare allocation, transit access, or any other zone-level administrative service during the review period. All existing [[GLMZ]] authority structures remain in effect.
aftermath: The Class II application stalled at UNCA within four months of filing when Ironclad and Ringo submitted a formal competing petition arguing that zone redesignation required unanimous Big 20 consent — a provision that does not appear in the UNCA Class II framework but that both corporations claim was implied in the original GLMZ formation compact of 2189. The EZA disputed this reading. The UNCA's North American Jurisdictions panel accepted the petition for review, pausing the main application timeline. The dispute remains unresolved.
runner_relevance: The redesignation fight created immediate contract work across the zone: corponations opposing the application need intelligence on which Big 20 members are wavering and what inducements are being offered; the EZA needs documentation of ungoverned zones that it officially pretends do not exist in order to address the supplemental filing; and the UNCA, poorly staffed for North American zone politics, has been quietly contracting local operators to provide ground-level reporting that its own observers cannot access. The unanimous-consent petition also created demand for archival research work — both the EZA and Ironclad's legal teams are paying for access to the 2189 formation compact's original negotiation records, some of which exist only in physical form in heavily restricted corporate archives.
